Lessons.Title: Fermi Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Build and critique approximate quantitative models for long travel, packing many cartons, and exterior tile coverage.

Fermi estimates begin with a question missing some physical measurements. Select assumptions, convert to matching units, compute a plausible range, and state why another student could obtain a different defensible result.

A cross-country ant journey requires distance and speed. A cereal-box warehouse requires actual usable stacking dimensions, not only total volume. A monument covering estimate requires surface area of all exposed faces, tile area and a plausible allowance for cut edges.

Original Edulytiks examples below are illustrations, not observations or reproductions of source artworks. Original student-designed models, precision and competing assumptions require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate with uncertain inputs
KeyConcepts.Definition: A Fermi question asks for a plausible scale of an unfamiliar result, not one experimentally exact value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Document the approximations and vary one dominant assumption to test sensitivity.
KeyConcepts.Example: An ideal continuous ant-speed model differs from a route allowing rest and detours.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dimensional consistency
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rate relates compatible measurement units such as distance per time.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Convert kilometers to millimeters before dividing by a speed measured in millimeters per second.
KeyConcepts.Example: 3,900 km = 3.9 billion mm; at 20 mm/s time is 195 million seconds.

KeyConcepts.Title: Packing and covering
KeyConcepts.Definition: Volume capacity, physical carton fit, and exposed surface area are distinct geometric constraints.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check real box orientation and available floor dimensions; for tiles count all included faces and allow for edge waste.
KeyConcepts.Example: Two billion hypothetical 0.125-ft³ cereal cartons need at least 250 million ft³ before any wasted space.

WorkedExamples.Title: How long could an ant take?
WorkedExamples.Question: Under deliberately simplified assumptions, how long to cover a 3,900-km path at 20 mm/s continuously?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide compatible distance by speed; retain uncertainty caveats.
Steps: Convert 3,900 km to 3,900,000,000 mm.
Divide by 20 mm/s to get 195,000,000 seconds.
Divide by 86,400 seconds/day for about 2,257 days.
Divide by 365 days/year to obtain approximately 6.2 years.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Approximately 6.2 continuous years in the ideal model, not a prediction of an actual ant journey.
WorkedExamples.Check: A 10% change in speed produces a substantial change in travel time; stops, lifespan, and real obstacles are excluded.

WorkedExamples.Title: Pack an illustrative cereal warehouse
WorkedExamples.Question: Model storage of 2 billion boxes each 0.25-by-0.5-by-1 ft in a warehouse 10 ft tall.
WorkedExamples.Method: Model carton volume, floor area, and integer packing alignment.
Steps: Each carton volume is 0.25×0.5×1 = 0.125 ft³.
Total carton volume is 2,000,000,000×0.125 = 250,000,000 ft³.
Ideal floor area at 10 ft high is 25,000,000 ft².
A hypothetical 5,000-by-5,000-ft floor and a 20,000-by-10,000-by-10 aligned carton arrangement fit the assumed count without aisles.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One idealized floor is 5,000 by 5,000 ft; practical warehouses need space for aisles and non-ideal stacking.
WorkedExamples.Check: A floor with an arbitrarily tiny width could have the correct area and still fail to fit the cartons.

WorkedExamples.Title: Estimate monument exterior tile coverage
WorkedExamples.Question: Create a labeled model of a tall monument using four trapezoidal faces and triangular top faces. Estimate the tiles needed.
WorkedExamples.Method: Student-defined geometric assumptions and teacher-reviewed open-ended evidence.
Steps: Identify exterior faces including those hidden from a single viewpoint.
Estimate or research appropriate dimensions with dated/credible sources.
Decompose trapezoids into measurable rectangles/triangles, and add the exposed face areas.
Choose the tile area and estimate edge losses or waste; provide a range.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The numerical estimate depends on explicitly chosen dimensions, tile size, rounding and waste assumptions.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher verifies face inventory, consistent square units, realistic assumptions and supported variation. One number is not sufficient.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mixing speed and distance units before division.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: km divided by mm/s without conversion does not yield the intended seconds.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use consistent distance units and check that the compound units reduce to time.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming sufficient volume proves feasible physical packing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Too-narrow dimensions can block storage even when the total space is large enough.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check integer carton fit along every proposed warehouse edge and account for realistic clearance.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Estimating tile coverage from only visible monument faces.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A photograph shows only some of the exterior and cuts may waste tiles.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Include the entire intended exterior and explicitly estimate edge waste.

SummaryPoints: Fermi estimates use assumptions, unit conversion and defensible uncertainty ranges.
Physical packing constraints differ from abstract volume or floor area.
Open-ended designs and justifications need human evaluation.

Visuals.Title: Three Fermi modeling pathways
Visuals.Description: Text-accessible strategy organizer: a three-row comparison linking ant journey to distance/speed and time units, cereal storage to count×carton volume plus integer packing constraints, and monument tiles to exposed trapezoid/triangle face areas divided by tile area, adjusted for edge waste. No publisher artwork is used.
Visuals.SecondaryLabel: Count × volume; exposed area ÷ tile area
Items: Cereal boxes: capacity and feasible layers
Monument: shaded exterior including hidden faces
SecondaryItems: Explain why no one exact answer

Lessons.Title: If Our Class Were the World
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Model a historical world-population distribution in a hypothetical class and justify fractional percentages, rounding and original visual displays.

The public 2017–2019 curriculum describes a historical 7.4-billion-person world using 30 representative classmates. This is a dated source-era premise, not a current-world-population statistic. Convert category counts into percentages and scale a source-referenced proportion to other hypothetical class sizes.

A modeled fraction of a person cannot appear in a classroom diagram. Rounded counts need explanatory choices, and independently selected characteristics may overlap, so they are not automatically a disjoint partition.
Classroom model data do not describe the actual identities or private demographics of real students. Original research questions, visual representations and interpretations require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Population as a hypothetical class
KeyConcepts.Definition: A smaller group can model a much larger reference population through approximate equivalent ratios.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Scale a known fraction or percentage to a chosen imaginary class size.
KeyConcepts.Example: 12 of 30 represents 12/30 = 40% in a dated teaching model.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number representations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Individual represented people are whole count units, not fractional people.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Report plausible integer approximations and how their percentages deviate from the reference value.
KeyConcepts.Example: 10% of a 25-person model gives 2.5; selecting 2 (8%) or 3 (12%) needs an explicit approximation rule.

KeyConcepts.Title: Interpret and present source data
KeyConcepts.Definition: A visual class model must cite the date and sources used for the representative population measures.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep the same whole for each proportion, avoid summing overlapping attributes, and label the chart or accessible table.
KeyConcepts.Example: The historical lesson's sample numbers cannot be presented as verified 2026 world demographics.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use the dated 30-class model
WorkedExamples.Question: A historical illustrative 30-person model assigns 14 to one food characteristic, 12 to the under-20 group, and 5 to a region. What are the complement, age percent, and region proportion?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the model categories against the same whole of 30 and label its historical nature.
Steps: The complement of the first group is 30−14=16 classmates.
The under-20 proportion is 12/30=2/5=40%.
The hypothetical regional proportion is 5/30=1/6≈16.7%.
If applied to an explicitly dated 7.4-billion premise, that fraction would represent about 1.23 billion, not a current verified regional population.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The complement is 16 model classmates; the second group is 40%; the regional share is approximately 16.7% of this historical model.
WorkedExamples.Check: No category is assumed disjoint from age or food choices, and the dated world value is not modernized without a source.

WorkedExamples.Title: Round an approximate class model
WorkedExamples.Question: Suppose a documented/reference example gives a characteristic prevalence of 10%. How can a 25-person model show it?
WorkedExamples.Method: Calculate the expected count and compare two nearby integer approximations.
Steps: Compute 0.10×25=2.5 expected model people.
Choose two or three entire represented people, not 2.5.
Two people out of 25 is 8%; three out of 25 is 12%.
State why both are two percentage points from the 10% target and what rounding rule is used.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Either 2 or 3 imaginary classmates is a defensible approximate 10% model under a stated choice.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original poster/drawing and choice of approximation require teacher review; there is no uniquely correct visual.

WorkedExamples.Title: Design a hypothetical world-class display
WorkedExamples.Question: Develop two population research questions, cite dated statistics or state invented illustration premises, and present a scaled 30-person class diagram.
WorkedExamples.Method: Student-selected research, modeling and teacher-reviewed visual communication.
Steps: State two well-posed population questions and the data source/date for each.
Use equivalent ratios to compute hypothetical whole-person representation counts.
Explain integer rounding and how overlapping attributes are handled.
Create a labeled original visual display with a text alternative and evaluate its limitations.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Several diagrams and population categories are valid when sourced, consistently scaled, labeled and justified.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks research integrity, ratios, count plausibility, graphic accessibility and explanation. No single numeric verifier replaces this assessment.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating historical world numbers as up-to-date facts.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The lesson's source-era 7.4-billion model is explicitly dated.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label the reference year/model and verify any actual current statistic separately.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Showing 2.5 people or summing overlapping population attributes as disjoint groups.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Class counts must be integers and people may fit several categories.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose justified rounded counts and model each overlapping characteristic separately.

SummaryPoints: Population-to-class ratios are hypothetical models that require reference source and date.
Translate percentages to whole-person approximate counts with transparent rounding.
Teacher-reviewed questions and original visual reports cannot be fully evaluated by one numeric answer.

Visuals.Title: Historical population model: 30 classmates
Visuals.Description: Text-accessible example comparing historically stated 14 out of 30 people with its complement 16, an under-20 group of 12 out of 30 corresponding to 40%, and a modeled regional group of 5 out of 30 near 16.7%. These categories can overlap, and the original lesson's 7.4-billion number is an historical source premise, not a current data report.
SecondaryItems: Do not assert real class identities
